---
title: Under the Hood
type: experiment
order: 80
---

Three stages, chained by `quarto render`, each owned by a different
runtime. None of them ever rewrite your page source:

1. **Pre-render (Python, once per build).** Quarto's `project.pre-render`
   hook runs a script that scans every page in the project. It's a full
   scan every time, even when Quarto is only rendering one page, because
   that page still needs to resolve links against every *other* page.
   The script parses each page's `title:`, `also-known-as:`, `type:`, and
   `quarto-graph:` frontmatter, scans its body for double-bracketed
   wikilinks and for plain Markdown links that resolve to another project
   page, and builds a registry (name → page) and a backlink map (page →
   pages that link to it). It also reads the project's own `_quarto.yml`
   for a project-wide `quarto-graph:` default — a new read source; earlier
   versions of this pass never opened `_quarto.yml` at all — and folds
   that with each page's own `quarto-graph:` override into a per-page
   `sidebar` config (`{enabled, depth}`, field-level merge, see
   [[The Graph Widget]]). That registry is written to a JSON side-channel
   file. The page source itself is never touched.
2. **Render (Pandoc, once per page).** Quarto renders each real `.qmd`
   normally. A registered Lua filter reads that side-channel registry once
   and, for this one page's in-memory document only: rewrites
   wikilinks into real links (see [[Wikilinks and Aliases]]),
   appends this page's own "## Backlinks" section (see [[Backlinks]]), and
   records this page's own real output URL to another small side-channel
   file. If this page's own resolved sidebar config (from the registry) has
   `enabled: false`, the filter stamps
   `<meta name="quarto-graph-sidebar" content="false">` into this page's
   `<head>`; if it's enabled with a `depth` other than the default of 1, it
   instead stamps `<meta name="quarto-graph-sidebar-depth" content="N">`,
   a per-page fact, injected the same way as backlinks, not routed through
   `graph.json` (see [[The Graph Widget]]). The same filter
   also attaches `graph.js`/`graph.css` via `quarto.doc.add_html_dependency`,
   which is how they get a correct relative path regardless of how deeply
   nested the page is.
3. **Post-render (Python, once per build).** Quarto's `project.post-render`
   hook runs once every page has rendered, joins the pre-render registry
   with every page's own recorded real output URL, and writes `graph.json`
   directly into the output directory.

## Why nothing computes a page's own output URL

A resolved wikilink is just a relative link to the target page's own
*source* path (e.g. `/getting-started.qmd`). Quarto's own project link
rewriting turns that into whatever the real final URL is, honoring
whatever output conventions your project already uses. This project has
no output-path convention of its own to get wrong, because it never
computes one. [[The Graph Widget]]'s `graph.json` is the one place a real
URL is needed. Client-side JS reads it directly, so Quarto's own link
rewriting can't help there. Instead it's read from `quarto.doc.output_file`
after the fact, per page, rather than predicted.

## Two ways an extension reaches into a project, and they're not the same

`_extensions/quarto-graph/_extension.yml` contributes two different
things, and only one applies automatically:

| Contribution | Applies to your `_quarto.yml` | You still have to write |
|---|---|---|
| `contributes.project` | automatically, the moment `project: type: quarto-graph` names the extension | nothing |
| `contributes.filters` | **not automatically** | `filters: [quarto-graph]`, explicitly |

This was confirmed empirically, not just read off the Quarto docs: a
debug print inside the filter stayed silent on every render until
`filters: [quarto-graph]` was added to the consuming `_quarto.yml`.

## The Python/Lua duplication seam

The pre-render pass (Python) and the per-page filter (Lua) each parse
wikilink syntax independently. Python builds the backlink map up front.
Lua rewrites links at render time, because a Lua filter can only see the
one page it's rendering, not the whole project. That's two
implementations of the same bracket-syntax grammar, in two languages,
kept in sync by hand. There's no way around it inside this two-runtime
architecture. It's a real, permanent seam, not an oversight.

Markdown links don't share this seam. Only Python parses them, to fold
their targets into the backlink map ([[Wikilinks and Aliases]]). A plain
Markdown link is already a real Pandoc link by the time Lua sees it, so
there's nothing for the filter to rewrite — it passes through untouched,
same as any other link Lua doesn't recognize as a wikilink.

## Two ways the mini-panel decides not to show up

There's no `quarto-graph: sidebar:` check anywhere for `page-layout: full`,
`toc: false`, book vs. website projects, or non-HTML formats like
`revealjs`/`pdf`/`dashboard` — none of those are special-cased, on purpose.

`graph.js`'s `mountLocalPanel` looks for the right-margin container
(`#quarto-margin-sidebar`, or the mkdocs-material equivalent) with
`document.querySelector` at runtime, and does nothing if it isn't there.
That single check is already correct for every layout Quarto can produce,
present or future, because it asks "does this container physically exist
right now," not "which layout keyword produced this page." A
`page-layout: full` page, a `toc: false` page, a custom grid, a `revealjs`
slide deck (which never even loads `graph.js`) — all handled the same way,
for free.

The `quarto-graph: sidebar:` config from the previous section is a
different, independent check: the container exists, but the user doesn't
want the panel there. That's why it's a separate mechanism (a meta tag
checked before the `graph.json` fetch) rather than folded into the same
container lookup — one answers "is there room for this," the other answers
"do you want it here."

## Strict mode

The pre-render script accepts `--strict`, which turns any unresolved
wikilink into a build failure instead of just a warning. The default
`pre-render` line in `_extension.yml` (just `prerender.py`) is auto-resolved
by Quarto against wherever the extension actually got installed, so it
can't carry extra arguments. To enable `--strict`, replace that line in your
installed copy with an explicit command pointing at its real path, e.g.
`python3 _extensions/wvictor14/quarto-graph/prerender.py --strict` if you
installed via `quarto add wvictor14/quarto-graph` — check your project's
`_extensions/` folder for the exact path if you installed it differently.
